content.headline: A Limb-Sparing Option for Bone Cancer in Dogs
content.tagline: A personalized 3D-printed implant designed to replace bone and help your dog keep their leg
content.description:
This study is evaluating a new limb-sparing surgery for dogs with bone cancer (osteosarcoma). Instead of removing the limb, this approach uses a custom 3D-printed implant to replace the diseased bone.

The implant is designed specifically for your dog using advanced imaging and is made from a material that can gradually be replaced by your dog’s own bone over time. The goal is to maintain limb function while treating the cancer.

Dogs in this study will undergo surgery followed by chemotherapy and long-term monitoring to evaluate how well the implant works and how the cancer responds to treatment.
content.requirements:
1. Initial testing to confirm eligibility
  2. Whole-body PET-CT scan to design the implant
  3. Limb-sparing surgery and hospitalization
  4. Chemotherapy every 3 weeks for 6 treatments
  5. Follow-up visits including:
  6. Bloodwork
  7. Orthopedic exams and gait analysis
  8. X-rays of the limb and chest
  9. Ongoing monitoring every 2 months for up to 20 months
content.who_can_participate:
Dogs may qualify if they:

  1. Have suspected or confirmed osteosarcoma of the distal radius
  2. Meet criteria for limb-sparing surgery
  3. Are giant breed or weigh at least 88 lbs (40 kg)
  4. Have no evidence of cancer spread (metastasis)
  5. Are otherwise healthy
  6. Are not receiving medications that affect the immune system
content.benefits_and_risks:
Benefits:

  1. Access to an advanced limb-sparing surgical option
  2. Study covers major costs, including:
  3. PET-CT scan and anesthesia
  4. Custom 3D-printed implant
  5. Surgery and hospitalization
  6. Chemotherapy and follow-up imaging for up to 20 months
  7. Up to $5,825 coverage for surgical complications
  8. Contribute to research that may improve treatment for bone cancer in dogs

Risks:

  1. Risks associated with major surgery and anesthesia
  2. Possible complications from the implant or healing process
  3. Side effects from chemotherapy
  4. Long-term commitment for follow-up care
  5. Treatment may not be successful
content.time_commitment: Initial surgery and chemotherapy over several months, with follow-up visits every 2 months for up to 20 months
content.compensation: Study covers surgery, implant, chemotherapy, and follow-up care, with additional support for complications
content.responsibilities:
1. Cover the cost of initial diagnostic testing and any additional tests recommended by your veterinarian
  2. Cover costs of complications beyond what the study provides
  3. Bring your dog to all required study appointments, including bandage changes (expected to be needed every 1-5 days for 2+ weeks after surgery)
  4. Cover costs of any visits performed outside CSU
  5. Agree to provide the limb to study personnel after your dog passes away or is euthanized
